Earlier this year, when Apple launched the MacBook Neo, the entire PC market was caught off guard. Although the aggressive pricing strategy of that laptop has since been forced to adjust in response to market conditions, just a few months later, competitors running Windows have陆续 announcing their respective counterattack products. Today it's HP's turn to make a move, launching a new-positioning laptop equipped with an OLED screen, with a starting price also set at US$699, though there are quite a few conditions attached behind it.

The HP OmniBook 5 14 looks like a low-cost, colourful body similar to the MacBook Neo, mixed with the more refined, understated green and blue of Apple's iPad Air series. The body is just 11.77mm thin, and the 14-inch screen version weighs only 2.56 pounds, which would normally be a very suitable choice for the upcoming back-to-school shopping season — unfortunately, HP has almost missed that window. The real star of the show is actually that 14-inch screen — at this price point, HP has abandoned the common IPS panel and instead offers two OLED screen options, which will be discussed in detail later. The sides of the body feature two "full-function" USB-C ports and a headphone jack; when you open the screen, an FHD camera supporting Windows Hello greets you.

In terms of specifications, HP says it can support up to an Intel Core 7 processor, but the units currently on display only offer this option. Battery life sounds impressive on paper — up to 42 hours of local video playback — but the battery capacity has not been disclosed; honestly though, local video playback tests may not truly reflect real-world usage. HP mentions it is compatible with the company's own 65W mini GaN charger, and I assume the charger comes included in the box. Apart from that, it features dual microphones and audio tuned by "Poly Studio" — that is currently all the information known about this device. If you feel there's still a lot of information unclear, you're not alone.

First of all, it's not yet clear which processor the US$700 version will use, making it difficult to directly compare with Apple's A18 Pro. HP has simply not disclosed any information about storage and memory configurations at all — not even words like "up to" — which precisely reflects how heavily the PC market is being squeezed under the current tight RAM supply situation. Even the biggest selling point of this laptop comes with a rather daunting detail: HP spent considerable space in its announcement introducing the 2.5K OLED screen, but that version won't ship until March 2027. The version going on sale at Best Buy later this month will feature a 2K OLED screen, with brightness dropping sharply from 650 nits to just 300 nits.

There are still many unanswered questions, and some of the answers are disappointing. However, if HP has still managed to catch your attention, stay tuned for more details before the product officially goes on sale.
